lead: Prestressed concrete puts a beam or slab into compression before it carries load, so the concrete does not crack early. This unit explains the materials, the stressing systems, the stress calculations, the losses and the flexural and end-block design. After it you can compute prestress stresses, estimate losses, design a simple prestressed flexural member and read anchorage-zone details.
about: Chapter 6.1 gives the basic principle: a stretched tendon compresses concrete and cancels part of the bending tension. Chapter 6.2 explains why high-strength concrete and high-tensile steel are needed. Chapter 6.3 compares pre-tensioning and post-tensioning. Chapter 6.4 builds the stress formula and the load-balancing idea. Chapter 6.5 lists the losses that reduce the jacking force. Chapter 6.6 uses the effective force for flexural design. Chapter 6.7 designs the end block around the anchorage. Chapter 6.8 treats concordant cables in continuous members. Chapter 6.9 introduces partial prestressing, where tendons and ordinary bars work together.

chapters.idea: A prestressed member carries load with a pre-applied compression that keeps concrete from cracking in tension.
chapters.depth: Cover pre-compression, tendon and eccentricity, the internal couple, decompression and cracking, advantages such as smaller sections and longer spans, and the difference from ordinary reinforced concrete. Introduce the words tendon, jacking force and transfer. Mention pre-tensioned and post-tensioned only as names here.

figure.title: How prestress works
figure.aria: A stretched tendon pre-compresses the concrete, and later load cancels part of the bending tension so cracking is delayed.

chapters.example: A rectangular beam 200 mm × 400 mm carries a concentric tendon force P = 400 kN. Find the uniform stress. A = 200 × 400 = 80,000 mm²; f = P/A = 400,000 / 80,000 = 5 N/mm² compression. If a sagging moment later causes 8 N/mm² tension at the bottom, the net bottom stress is 8 − 5 = 3 N/mm² tension.
chapters.trap: Thinking prestress makes concrete tensile-strong. Prestress only adds compression; tension can still occur and must be checked.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 concrete properties; Unit 2 simple bending stress f = My/I.

chapters.idea: Prestressing forces are large, so the concrete must be strong and the steel must carry high tensile stress without yielding.
chapters.depth: Concrete grades M40 and above, cube and tensile strength, modulus, why high bearing and bond stresses need strong concrete. High-tensile steel as wires, strands and bars; 7-wire strand; stress-strain curve without a yield plateau; 0.1% proof stress; relaxation as a property. Keep numbers typical and qualitative.

figure.aria: Two material layers: high-strength concrete grade M40 and above, and high-tensile steel in wires, strands and bars.

chapters.example: A tendon has area Ap = 100 mm² and is stressed to 1600 N/mm². Find the force. P = 100 × 1600 = 160,000 N = 160 kN. If the same force were carried by mild steel at 250 N/mm², the area needed would be 160,000 / 250 = 640 mm².
chapters.trap: Using mild-steel yield stress as the design strength of high-tensile steel; it has no clear yield point, so use proof stress.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 stress-strain behaviour of concrete and steel; 6.1.
chapters.leave: Relaxation loss calculation to 6.5; anchorage bearing to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Pre-tensioning stresses the tendon before concrete is cast; post-tensioning stresses it after the concrete hardens.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Long-line and mould methods for pre-tensioning; ducts, anchorages, grouting and couplers for post-tensioning; bonded and unbonded tendons; names of common post-tensioning systems as examples. Compare transfer by bond and by end anchorage.

figure.aria: Timeline comparing pre-tensioning, where the tendon is stressed before casting, and post-tensioning, where stressing comes after casting and is followed by grouting.

chapters.example: A post-tensioned beam has 4 tendons. Each tendon is jacked to 150 kN. Find the total jacking force. P = 4 × 150 = 600 kN. If the first tendon loses 3% force when the second is stressed, its force after that step is 150 × 0.97 = 145.5 kN.
chapters.trap: Saying post-tensioning transfers force by bond at the ends; initial transfer is by anchorage, and grouting only later provides bond.
chapters.leave: Loss details to 6.5; end block to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Stresses at any point are found by adding axial, prestress bending and load bending; load balancing chooses a tendon profile whose upward force cancels part of the load.
chapters.depth: Sign convention, f = P/A ± P e y/I ± M y/I; section modulus Z = I/y; top and bottom stresses at transfer and service; decompression and cracking moments; equivalent upward load for parabolic tendon w_p = 8 P e / L²; load balancing as a design aid.

figure.title: Superposition of stresses
figure.aria: Three stress parts, axial compression, prestress bending and load bending, are added to get the top and bottom stresses.

chapters.example: Beam b = 250 mm, D = 600 mm, A = 150,000 mm², I = 4.5 × 10⁹ mm⁴, Z = 15 × 10⁶ mm³. P = 600 kN at e = 150 mm below centroid. Find top and bottom stresses at transfer. P/A = 4 N/mm². P e / Z = 600,000 × 150 / 15,000,000 = 6 N/mm². Top = 4 − 6 = 2 N/mm² tension; bottom = 4 + 6 = 10 N/mm² compression. A sagging moment 120 kNm adds M/Z = 120,000,000 / 15,000,000 = 8 N/mm²: top 8 compression, bottom 8 tension. Net top = 6 compression; net bottom = 2 compression.
chapters.trap: Mixing signs; decide compression positive or negative and keep it for the whole calculation.

chapters.idea: The jacking force is not the force that stays; elastic shortening, friction, anchorage slip, creep, shrinkage and relaxation reduce it.
chapters.depth: List each loss, when it occurs, and its simple formula. Elastic shortening, friction P_x = P0 e^(−(μα + kx)), anchorage slip, creep, shrinkage and relaxation. Total effective prestress. Keep code factors qualitative.

figure.aria: The prestress force starts at 100 percent at jacking and falls in steps to 80 percent after twelve months as losses accumulate.

chapters.example: A post-tensioned beam is jacked to P0 = 1000 kN. For this example take friction 4%, anchorage slip 3%, elastic shortening 2%, creep 6%, shrinkage 3% and relaxation 2% of P0. Find total loss and effective force. Total = 4+3+2+6+3+2 = 20%. Loss = 0.20 × 1000 = 200 kN. Effective P = 800 kN.
chapters.trap: Adding losses in the wrong order; for a simple estimate add percentages of the initial force, but state the assumption.
chapters.leave: Design checks using effective force to 6.6.

chapters.idea: Flexural design checks service stresses with effective prestress and ultimate moment with tendon strength and code stress block.
chapters.depth: Working stress checks at transfer and service: no tension or limited tension; allowable compressive stress. Ultimate moment for bonded tendons: equilibrium 0.36 fck b xu = Ap fpb, Mu = Ap fpb (d − 0.42 xu) for a rectangular section; mention flanged sections and mild steel addition. Type 1, 2, 3 behaviour names. Keep shear and deflection as checks only.

figure.title: Flexural design checks
figure.aria: Design flow from section and tendon choice through transfer and service stress checks to the ultimate moment check.

chapters.trap: Using the effective prestress force directly as the ultimate capacity; ultimate capacity depends on tendon area and its high tensile stress, not only on P.
chapters.leave: Shear and torsion to Unit 3; deflection to Unit 2 serviceability.

chapters.idea: A concentrated anchorage force spreads into the beam and creates transverse bursting and spalling stresses that need end-block reinforcement.
chapters.depth: Bearing stress under the plate; primary and secondary anchorage zones; bursting force; spalling near the surface; transverse reinforcement layout; check bearing plate size. Use simple approximate formulas, not code clause numbers.

figure.title: Anchorage zone action
figure.aria: A jack force passes through a bearing plate and spreads into the end block, producing transverse bursting tension that needs closed stirrups.

chapters.example: An anchorage force P = 1000 kN acts on a square plate 200 mm × 200 mm at the end of a beam 600 mm wide. Find bearing stress and an approximate bursting force. Bearing stress = 1,000,000 / (200 × 200) = 25 N/mm². Using Fbst ≈ 0.25 P (1 − a/b) with a = 200 mm and b = 600 mm: Fbst ≈ 250 × (1 − 0.333) = 166.7 kN.
chapters.trap: Designing end-block steel as flexural steel; it is transverse splitting reinforcement, and the bearing plate size controls concrete bearing stress.

chapters.idea: A concordant cable gives no reactions from prestress in a continuous member; linear transformation moves its profile without changing equivalent loads.
chapters.depth: Definitions of concordant cable, pressure line, linear transformation; why a concordant profile is useful; how adding a straight line changes eccentricities but not curvature; continuous beams. Keep to two-span examples.

figure.title: Linear transformation
figure.aria: Adding a straight line to a cable profile changes eccentricity but not curvature, so the equivalent upward load and the reactions stay the same.

chapters.example: A parabolic tendon in a span L = 12 m has midspan eccentricity e = 120 mm and P = 800 kN. Find the equivalent upward load. w_p = 8 P e / L² = 8 × 800,000 × 0.120 / 144 = 5333 N/m ≈ 5.33 kN/m. Adding a straight line e_t = k x/L has zero second derivative, so w_p stays 5.33 kN/m.
chapters.trap: Confusing concordant with straight or concentric; concordant means zero prestress reactions, not zero eccentricity.

chapters.idea: Partial prestressing uses tendons plus ordinary reinforcement so that prestress and rebar share the required strength and crack control.
chapters.depth: Definition, prestress ratio, full versus partial versus RC, serviceability and crack control, economy, common uses. Design idea: prestress carries part of moment, rebar carries the rest; check stresses and ultimate strength.

figure.aria: A spectrum from full prestressing with no tension, through partial prestressing with tendons and ordinary bars, to ordinary reinforced concrete.

chapters.example: A beam must resist Mu = 300 kNm. Prestress is designed to contribute 180 kNm and ordinary steel 120 kNm. With fy = 415 N/mm² and lever arm 600 mm, find As. As = 120 × 10⁶ / (0.87 × 415 × 600) = 554 mm².
chapters.trap: Treating partial prestressing as a lower grade of full prestressing; it is a deliberate mix, and crack width and ultimate strength both need checks.
chapters.leave: Detailed crack-width calculation to Unit 2 serviceability.

links: partial prestress combines tendon and rebar
